question_type: two-endpoint growth metrics (CAGR, decay factor, 'arc elasticity') from one agency column of an annual outlays table; the third metric's definition is the whole question
decisive_step: FORMULA, not retrieval: every cell and the reference found the same table (FFO-3 'On-Budget and Off-Budget Outlays by Agency', Department of Labor column (13), FY2011 and FY2019 rows, latest revision of FY2011) and agreed on CAGR and decay factor (= 1 + CAGR). The split is what 'arc elasticity (using midpoint percentage change)' means when the question supplies only ONE series. The answer key accepts the midpoint percentage change of outlays by itself (what c computed at c[36] and chose at c[39]). a, b, b2 and the reference divided that by the midpoint percentage change of the fiscal-year number (a few tenths of a percent), producing a value hundreds of times larger in magnitude. The reference made this decision in worklog.md Step 4 / calc.py line `arc = pct_q_mid / pct_y_mid`, listed the 'midpoint %dQ alone' reading only as an alternative in Step 5, and was graded wrong (correct.opus = 0).

smallest_change.change: Add to the working advice: 'Definitions: when the question names a measure and adds a parenthetical method (for example "arc elasticity (using midpoint percentage change)"), compute exactly the quantity the parenthetical describes from the series the question gives. Do not add a second variable the question does not name (such as the year number, or time) to make a textbook formula fit. If one value of a multi-value answer comes out hundreds of times larger than its siblings, that is a sign you introduced such a variable: recompute with the parenthetical's definition.'
smallest_change.could_hurt_right_cells: unlikely: it only fires when a parenthetical method is present and the question gives one series; c already behaves this way, and on ordinary two-variable elasticity questions the second variable is named so the sentence does not apply

fix.why_not_text: n/a (fix is TEXT). Note that a's text had no sentence about metric definitions at all; the relevant deliberation (a[25], b2[33], b2[35]) shows the model was uncertain and looking for a rule, which is exactly what a sentence can supply.
fix.irreducible: Partly. The question misuses 'arc elasticity' (an elasticity needs two variables) and the stronger reference solver, with full reasoning, chose the textbook definition and was graded wrong; the accepted reading is a question-writer convention ('the parenthetical is the definition'). That convention is learnable and general enough to state as text, but a well-reasoned model can still legitimately disagree, so confidence is medium, not high. issue47 is false, so the key is not formally disputed.

A v10 tool improvement: tag FFO-4 columns with the fiscal year and completeness they cover (e.g. 'This fiscal year to date (FY2011, full year in the Sept-data issue)') so printings can be asked for --period FY2011 on such tables; a[19] and c[21] each had to infer by hand which issue holds the full year. 3) show_table --grep matches row labels only; three cells grepped a column name and got 0 rows (b[14], c[11], c[27]). Cheap tool fix: when --grep matches no row but matches a column header, print 'no row matched X; X is column c13 (Department of Labor (13)): use --cols 13'. 4) --cols numbering: b[16] and c[29] asked for column 14 expecting Labor (13) and got a stitched part-2 column; the header lists v13 = c13, and the confusion between the printed '(13)' suffix, c-index and v-index cost a step each time. 5) The OfficeQACorpus.search python API prints an object whose iteration yields field names (b[6], b[9]); if it stays in the environment its __iter__/__repr__ should print hits. 6) Cost: b2 used 23 requests / 527k input tokens versus a's 13 / 195k for the same wrong answer, mostly on FFO-3 vs FFO-4 verification (b2[35]-[42]) that a settled in one printings comparison (a[23]); the 'several tables look alike' advice can be expensive when the tool could state the identity itself (e.g. a printings/show_table note 'FFO-3 agency columns = FFO-4 Total funds (4)/(8) for the same FY').
